title: The snowstorm behind the preacher
hookLine: Emerson recalls a sermon so hollow that the real snow falling outside the window preached better (Divinity School Address)

lines: THE SNOW IS WHAT HE REMEMBERED.
cards: Ralph Waldo Emerson once sat through a sermon so lifeless, he says, that it nearly tempted him to stop going to church altogether. The minister went on, correct and hollow.
Behind him was a window, and through the window, snow was falling. Emerson's eye kept leaving the pulpit for the weather.
Later, standing in front of a room of young men about to become ministers themselves, he told them about that sermon. What he remembered was the snow.

teach.b: First, the line itself. The talk is known as the Divinity School Address, given at Harvard.

A snow storm was falling around them, Emerson says, and then comes the sentence: "The snow storm was real; the preacher merely spectral." Spectral: like a ghost, there and not there. Second, what was missing.
You couldn't tell from the sermon, Emerson says, that the man had ever lived. Not one word hinted that he had laughed or cried, married or fallen in love, been praised or cheated or embarrassed.
Whatever his life had taught him, none of it made it into the room. Third, what Emerson wanted instead.

teach.h: NOT ONE WORD OF HIS OWN LIFE.
teach.b: A true preacher, he says, hands out his own life to people, life passed through the fire of thought.
And to be fair: in the same address he calls the Sabbath and the institution of preaching two great gifts Christianity gave the world. His complaint is not with church.
It's with a speaker who talks about holy things from a long way off. Fourth, why the snow. It didn't say anything.
It just fell, fully there, and so it taught better than the sermon did.
That's a test anyone can borrow: when you speak about what matters to you, does it come from what you've lived, or from what you've heard is the right thing to say? It's a high bar, and a plain one.

how: Readers of Emerson often return to the snowstorm passage as a test for any speaker or teacher: whether what they say has passed through their own life, or only through other people's words.

games.q: what does “the snowstorm behind the preacher” mean?
o: a storm that cut a church service short one winter
a sermon Emerson preached on the beauty of winter
real snow that taught more than a hollow sermon

games.q: inside the snowstorm passage: tap the pairs.

s: Emerson's complaint was with church itself
in the same address he calls the Sabbath and preaching two great gifts. his complaint was with a hollow speaker.
the sermon gave no hint the man had laughed or wept
Emerson says nothing in it showed the preacher had ever lived.
the snow taught by saying something wise
it said nothing. it was simply, fully there.

games.q: you're in the pews. the sermon is correct and lifeless. outside the window, snow is falling. where does your attention go?
o: back to the sermon, out of duty.
out the window, to the snow.
games.why: Emerson's went to the snow, and he remembered it: "the snow storm was real; the preacher merely spectral."

practice: Let your attention go to whatever is actually here, the way Emerson's went to the window: the weight of your body in the chair, a sound from outside, the air on your hands, the light.
No commentary, no meaning to find, just the plain fact of each thing, fully there, like snow falling. When a thought pulls you off, come back to one real thing.

wordCard.voice: The snowstorm behind the preacher. Emerson's memory of a hollow sermon, and the real snow falling past the window that said more than the man in the pulpit. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the snow was real. A plain thing, fully there, can teach. That's today, done.
